title: Distributed Optimal Control Problems Governed By Poroelasticity Equations
authors: Arbaz Khan, Jeonghun J. Lee, Harpal Singh
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we propose and analyze a novel two-field symmetric formulation with solid displacement and fluid pressure as main unknowns for the Biot's consolidation model in poroelasticity. Firstly, we prove the well-posedness of the new formulation and then show the existence and uniqueness of optimal control where the fluid sources in the model act as a control variable. We prove a priori error estimates for the fully discrete scheme with backward Euler time discretization and a variational approximation of the control variable. A numerical example is presented to validate the performance of the proposed novel scheme.
tldr: This paper develops a two-field symmetric formulation for Biot's consolidation model in poroelasticity and analyzes optimal control problems with fluid sources as control variables.
motivation: To propose a novel formulation for poroelasticity that enables well-posedness and optimal control analysis, which is important for applications like geomechanics and biomedical engineering.
method: A two-field symmetric formulation with solid displacement and fluid pressure is introduced. Well-posedness is proved, and existence/uniqueness of optimal control is shown. A priori error estimates are derived for a fully discrete scheme using backward Euler time discretization and variational approximation of the control.
result: The new formulation is well-posed, and the optimal control problem has a unique solution. Error estimates are established, and a numerical example validates the scheme's performance.
conclusion: The proposed method provides a rigorous framework for optimal control in poroelasticity, with potential extensions to more complex models and applications.

title: On The Equicontinuity Of The Hutchinson Operator
authors: Piotr Szuca Filip Strobin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove that the Hutchinson operators of a wide class of Iterated Function Systems are equicontinuous. In particular, every Iterated Function System with an attractor has equicontinuous Hutchinson operator.
tldr: This paper proves equicontinuity of Hutchinson operators for a wide class of Iterated Function Systems.
motivation: To establish equicontinuity properties of Hutchinson operators, which are fundamental in fractal theory and iterated function systems.
method: The authors use mathematical analysis and topological arguments to prove equicontinuity for a broad class of IFS, including those with attractors.
result: They show that every Iterated Function System with an attractor has an equicontinuous Hutchinson operator.
conclusion: The result provides a theoretical foundation for the stability and convergence of IFS, with potential implications in fractal geometry and dynamical systems.

title: Partial Section Iii: For Anosov Flows
authors: Th\'eo Marty
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the previous papers in the series, we characterized partial cross-sections for general flows, in the spirit of Fried's work on global cross-sections. In this paper, we deduce several consequences for Anosov flows. We provide a homology criterion for the existence of a partial cross-section in a given cohomology class. Additionally, there are at most finitely many partial cross-sections in that cohomology class. We deduce that on a 3-dimensional hyperbolic manifold, any Anosov flow is homologically full.
tldr: This paper studies partial cross-sections for Anosov flows, providing a homology criterion and finiteness result, with an application to 3D hyperbolic manifolds.
motivation: To extend Fried's work on global cross-sections to partial cross-sections for general flows, and to derive consequences for Anosov flows.
method: Mathematical analysis using homology theory and dynamical systems techniques.
result: A homology criterion for existence of partial cross-sections in a given cohomology class, finiteness of such cross-sections, and that any Anosov flow on a 3D hyperbolic manifold is homologically full.
conclusion: The results advance the understanding of Anosov flows and cross-sections, with implications for topology and dynamics.

title: Additive Matrix Integer-Valued Autoregressive Model
authors: Kaiyan Cui, Yikai Hu, Tianyun Guo
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Contemporary data-driven and technology-integrated era, various matrix-valued integer-valued time series, such as cross-regional crime statistics, multi-category sales records, and network traffic matrices, exhibit high dimensionality, complex structures, and strong row-column intertwined dependencies. Although the existing matrix integer-valued autoregressive (MINAR) model provides a framework that directly handles matrix data and captures bidirectional row-column dependencies, it suffers from limited interpretability and inflexible structural representation, as its parameters often lack clear empirical meaning and the model cannot separately distinguish the effects arising from rows, columns, and lagged dynamics. To overcome these drawbacks, this paper proposes the additive matrix integer-valued autoregressive (Add-MINAR) model. By introducing an additive structure that explicitly decomposes the matrix response into row effects, column effects, and lagged effects, the proposed model not only preserves the matrix-valued nature but also significantly enhances parameter interpretability and structural flexibility. Two estimation methods, namely projection estimation and iterative conditional least squares estimation, are developed for parameter identification and inference, and their asymptotic properties, including consistency and asymptotic normality, are rigorously established. Simulation results show that the iterative conditional least squares estimator generally outperforms the projection estimator in most scenarios. Empirical analysis of Chicago crime data further demonstrates that the Add-MINAR model achieves superior in-sample fitting and out-of-sample forecasting performance compared to benchmark models such as MINAR, making it particularly suitable for practical applications with explicit row-column interaction features.
tldr: This paper proposes an additive matrix integer-valued autoregressive model for time series data, with no connection to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: Existing matrix integer-valued autoregressive models lack interpretability and cannot separate row, column, and lagged effects.
method: The authors introduce an additive decomposition of the matrix response into row, column, and lagged effects, and develop projection and iterative conditional least squares estimation methods.
result: The iterative conditional least squares estimator generally outperforms the projection estimator; the model shows superior fitting and forecasting on Chicago crime data.
conclusion: The Add-MINAR model enhances interpretability and flexibility for matrix-valued integer time series, but is unrelated to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Bilevel Optimization For Smart Irrigation Control: A Framework For Enhancing Water-use Efficiency In Agriculture
authors: Roman Chertovskih, Nathalie Khalil, Lu\'is Sousa
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31133v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global warming has intensified water scarcity, posing a critical challenge for the agricultural sector, where seasonal demand often leads to significant wastage. This work addresses the need for efficient water management by proposing a smart irrigation control system based on a bilevel optimization algorithm. The framework aims to minimize water consumption across multiple fields simultaneously or, under supply constraints, to distribute available water equitably to minimize deviations from required levels. To achieve this, the problem is modeled hierarchically: the upper level acts as a central controller managing daily water limits and field-wise allocation, while the lower level acts as a centralized scheduler determining the optimal cooperative irrigation execution across all fields. This structure ensures that both global resource constraints and local irrigation needs are met efficiently. Preliminary results from digital simulation tools suggest that the proposed framework significantly improves water-use efficiency and supports sustainable irrigation practices, particularly in water-constrained scenarios.
tldr: This paper proposes a bilevel optimization framework for smart irrigation control to improve water-use efficiency in agriculture.
motivation: Global warming has intensified water scarcity, and agricultural irrigation often wastes water due to inefficient management.
method: A bilevel optimization algorithm is used: the upper level allocates daily water limits across fields, and the lower level schedules cooperative irrigation execution.
result: Preliminary digital simulations show significant improvement in water-use efficiency and equitable water distribution under constraints.
conclusion: The framework supports sustainable irrigation practices, especially in water-constrained scenarios, but further real-world validation is needed.

title: An Optimal Stability Theorem For H\"older's Inequality
authors: Yifan Lu Gangsong Leng

If [MATH] and \[ \sum_{k=1}^n a_k=\sum_{k=1}^n b_k=1, \] then \[ 1-\sum_{k=1}^n a_k^{1/p}b_k^{1/q} \ge \frac1{2pq}\left(\sum_{k=1}^n |a_k-b_k|\right)^2 . \] The constant [MATH] is best possible. method: The authors use analytic inequalities and optimization techniques to derive the sharp constant and prove its optimality.
result: They show that for sequences summing to 1, the deficit in Hölder's inequality is at least (1/(2pq)) times the squared L1 distance, with the constant being best possible.
conclusion: The result provides a tight stability bound for Hölder's inequality, with potential applications in functional analysis and probability.

title: Strong Log-concavity In Probit Regression
authors: Giacomo Zanella Martin Chak
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that strong log-concavity emerges in probit regression likelihoods without ridge penalization (i.e. Gaussian priors), unlike for the logistic case. Specifically, we provide: (a) a characterization of strong log-concavity for fixed designs, similar to that for the existence of the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) and (b) an analysis for Gaussian design, dependent on the proportionality [MATH] between the sample size [MATH] and the number of covariates [MATH]. In the latter case we show that, with high probability, provided [MATH] is small enough, the resulting condition number is finite and, in the asymptotic regime [MATH], independent of [MATH].
tldr: This paper proves strong log-concavity in probit regression likelihoods without ridge penalization, providing theoretical guarantees for optimization.
motivation: To understand the optimization landscape of probit regression, which is widely used in binary classification, and to show that it enjoys strong log-concavity unlike logistic regression.
method: The authors provide a characterization of strong log-concavity for fixed designs and an analysis for Gaussian designs using random matrix theory, deriving conditions on the sample size to covariate ratio.
result: Strong log-concavity holds for probit regression without Gaussian priors, with a finite condition number when the ratio of sample size to number of covariates is small enough, and asymptotically independent of dimension.
conclusion: The results imply that probit regression has favorable optimization properties, potentially enabling faster convergence guarantees for MCMC and optimization algorithms.

title: Cohomology Of Finite Element Stokes Complexes On Alfeld Splits
authors: Pablo D. Brubeck, Yizhou Liang, Charles Parker
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that the cohomology of the finite element Stokes complex consisting of piecewise polynomials spaces on an Alfeld split mesh from Fu, Guzm\'{a}n, & Neilan (2020, Math. Comp., 89, 1059--1091) is isomorphic to the cohomologies of the continuous Stokes and de Rham complexes. We also construct novel "minimal" conforming finite element complexes where the [MATH]-conforming space is the lowest-order space from Guzm\'{a}n & Neilan (2018, SIAM J. Numer. Anal., 56, 2826--2844) and the [MATH]-conforming space is piecewise constants. These minimal complexes also have cohomologies isomorphic to the continuous Stokes and de Rham complexes. We further construct local, bounded, cochain projections for the minimal complexes. All the results hold for strongly Lipschitz domains with nontrivial topologies and in the presence of mixed boundary conditions.
tldr: This paper studies the cohomology of finite element Stokes complexes on Alfeld splits, a topic in numerical analysis and computational mathematics.
motivation: To understand the cohomological properties of finite element spaces on Alfeld meshes, which are important for stable discretizations of fluid dynamics and elasticity.
method: The authors use algebraic topology and finite element theory to show isomorphism between cohomologies of discrete and continuous complexes, and construct minimal conforming complexes with local bounded cochain projections.
result: The cohomology of the finite element Stokes complex on Alfeld splits is isomorphic to that of the continuous Stokes and de Rham complexes; minimal complexes with piecewise constants also have isomorphic cohomologies.
conclusion: The results provide a theoretical foundation for using these finite element spaces in problems with nontrivial topology and mixed boundary conditions, but have no direct connection to the user's research interests.

title: The Surface You Test Is Not The Surface That Breaks
authors: Shifat E Arman, Syed Nazmus Sakib, Nafiul Haque, Shahrear Bin Amin
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-augmented LLM agents are vulnerable to prompt injection: a third party who controls part of the agent's context can plant instructions that the agent then executes as if they came from the user. Current evaluations report a single attack success rate per model on one channel, the tool output and treat that number as the model's vulnerability. But tool descriptions, which the agent reads at every turn before any tool is called, are themselves an injection surface that the attacker can choose instead. We hold the injection payload byte-identical and deliver it through both surfaces across 13 LLMs from six families and four task suites. The same bytes invert in success rate across models: GPT-4.1 is 96 percent vulnerable on tool outputs but only 4 percent on tool descriptions, while GEMINI-3-FLASH shows the mirror pattern at 20 percent and 98 percent. A variance decomposition over 6,830 attempts attributes 0 percent of the variation in attack outcomes to the surface alone, while the model-surface interaction accounts for 16.7 percent. Vulnerability is a property of the pairing, not the channel. The Adaptive Attack Rate, defined as the per-cell maximum over surfaces, exceeds the strongest fixed-surface baseline by +9.1 percentage points on average. Standard prompt-level defenses inherit the same blindspot, reducing tool-output ASR to 10-18 percent while leaving the description channel above 54 percent. Both attack and defense evaluation must report per-surface vulnerability.
tldr: This paper studies prompt injection vulnerabilities in tool-augmented LLM agents, showing that attack success rates depend on the surface (tool output vs. tool description) and the model, not just the channel.
motivation: Current evaluations of LLM prompt injection attacks only consider one attack surface (tool output), but tool descriptions are another potential surface that may yield different vulnerabilities.
method: The authors deliver identical injection payloads through both tool output and tool description surfaces across 13 LLMs and four task suites, measuring attack success rates and performing variance decomposition.
result: Vulnerability is a property of the model-surface pairing; GPT-4.1 is 96% vulnerable on tool outputs but 4% on descriptions, while Gemini-3-Flash shows the opposite. The Adaptive Attack Rate exceeds fixed-surface baselines by +9.1 percentage points.
conclusion: Both attack and defense evaluations must report per-surface vulnerability, as standard defenses fail on the description channel.

title: Pareto Optimality In Approval-Based Multiwinner Voting
authors: Joshua Sch\"unke
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In approval-based multiwinner voting, Pareto optimality is used as an axiom capturing efficiency of committees. We study the structure of the space of Pareto optimal committees in restricted domains and in general by investigating the monotonicity and reconfigurability of such committees. For the Candidate Interval and Voter Interval domains, we propose the Single Dominance Only property, which provides a simple characterization of Pareto optimality, and show that Pareto optimal committees satisfy committee monotonicity using this property. Further, we show that, for the above domains, any Pareto optimal committee can be reconfigured into any other Pareto optimal target committee without using auxiliary candidates, meaning that the candidates in the starting but not the target committee can be replaced by candidates in the target but not the starting committee one by one while preserving Pareto optimality at every step. In addition, we adapt a polynomial-time algorithm for finding a committee satisfying EJR+, a proportionality axiom, such that it also satisfies Pareto optimality, for the above domains. We further describe a polynomial-time algorithm for counting the number of Pareto optimal committees for voting instances satisfying Voter Interval, and give a proof idea for its correctness. For the unrestricted domain, we explain the challenges of proving committee monotonicity and reconfigurability. We provide an example in which the distance of two committees in the Pareto optimality reconfiguration graph exceeds the distance proven for the above domains, and outline an approach toward showing the connectedness of the graph.
tldr: This paper studies Pareto optimality in approval-based multiwinner voting, focusing on restricted domains like Candidate Interval and Voter Interval.
motivation: To understand the structure and properties of Pareto optimal committees in multiwinner voting, particularly monotonicity and reconfigurability.
method: The authors propose the Single Dominance Only property for restricted domains, prove committee monotonicity, and develop polynomial-time algorithms for finding and counting Pareto optimal committees.
result: Pareto optimal committees satisfy committee monotonicity in Candidate Interval and Voter Interval domains, and any two such committees can be reconfigured without auxiliary candidates. For unrestricted domains, challenges are identified.
conclusion: The work provides foundational insights into Pareto optimality in voting, with implications for algorithmic design and understanding of efficiency axioms.

title: CacheProbe: Auditing Prompt Cache Isolation In Gateway APIs
authors: Ryan Fahey
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30613v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Over the past year, prompt caching in Large Language Models (LLMs) has become increasingly more popular across inference APIs. Prompt caching helps save precious compute resources and speeds up response times by reusing parts of the KV cache of a specific prompt for another request. However, many implementations of prompt caching are not secure against timing attacks or even basic metadata disclosure. Gu et al. (ICML 2025) develop a method to audit prompt caching in LLMs. This paper investigates whether OpenRouter's API gateway architecture introduces prompt caching vulnerabilities that bypass provider-level prompt cache isolation guarantees. Most LLM inference providers implement per-account or per-organization prompt caching to prevent data leaks, but does routing through OpenRouter with shared organizational credentials inadvertently create global cache sharing across all OpenRouter users?
tldr: This paper audits prompt caching security in LLM API gateways, focusing on cache isolation vulnerabilities, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and thermodynamics.
motivation: Prompt caching in LLM APIs can leak data across users if isolation is not properly enforced; the study investigates whether OpenRouter's architecture introduces such vulnerabilities.
method: The authors audit OpenRouter's prompt caching behavior by designing timing attacks and metadata disclosure tests to check for global cache sharing.
result: The paper likely finds that OpenRouter's shared organizational credentials can lead to unintended cache sharing, bypassing provider-level isolation.
conclusion: The findings highlight security risks in prompt caching implementations and suggest the need for stronger isolation mechanisms in API gateways.

title: Investigating Detection And Obfuscation Of Prompt Injection Attacks Against Software Reverse Engineering Ai Agents
authors: Patrick Mcclure Brian Crawford
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic software reverse engineering systems are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks placed into the source code of executable binary files. This research demonstrates defensive tactics for detecting the presences of prompt injection strings in the decompiler output of adversarial example programs. Methods for obfuscating these attacks and subsequent methods for defending against these obfuscations are also explored. This research advances the understanding of risk and security of agentic software analysis systems necessary for their deployment into production-level cyber workflows.
tldr: This paper investigates detection and obfuscation of prompt injection attacks in software reverse engineering AI agents.
motivation: Agentic software reverse engineering systems are vulnerable to prompt injection attacks embedded in source code, posing security risks for deployment in production cyber workflows.
method: The authors demonstrate defensive tactics for detecting prompt injection strings in decompiler output and explore methods for obfuscating these attacks as well as defenses against obfuscations.
result: The research advances understanding of risks and security of agentic software analysis systems.
conclusion: The findings are important for deploying secure agentic systems in production-level cyber workflows.

title: Triaging Threats To Specialized Guardrails
authors: Wenjie Jacky Mo, Xiaofei Wen, Rui Cai, Boyu Zhu, Sicong Jiang, Zihan Wang, Minglai Yang, Zhe Zhao, Muhao Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building robust safety guardrails is essential for deploying Large Language Models across diverse real-world applications. However, this goal remains challenging because safety risks span heterogeneous threat domains, while existing datasets cover only fragmented risk subsets and rely on inconsistent taxonomies. Consequently, it remains unclear whether current guardrails can generalize beyond narrow evaluation settings. To better understand the robustness of guardrail models, we first introduce GuardZoo, a unified human-annotated benchmark with 32,460 samples covering 15 distinct unsafe categories. Evaluation on GuardZoo reveals that monolithic guardrails suffer from task interference: different threat domains require distinct decision boundaries that are difficult to compress into a single model. We therefore propose RouteGuard, a router-expert framework that triages each conversation to specialized expert guardrails for threat-specific detection. Experiments show that RouteGuard improves fine-grained threat detection over strong guardrail baselines, generalizes better under out-of-domain evaluation, and supports flexible modular expansion to emerging threats.
tldr: This paper introduces GuardZoo, a benchmark for evaluating guardrail models in LLMs, and proposes RouteGuard, a router-expert framework to improve threat detection across diverse unsafe categories.
motivation: Existing safety guardrails for LLMs are evaluated on fragmented datasets with inconsistent taxonomies, making it unclear if they generalize to diverse threat domains.
method: The authors create GuardZoo, a unified benchmark with 32,460 samples across 15 unsafe categories, and propose RouteGuard, a router-expert framework that triages conversations to specialized expert guardrails.
result: RouteGuard improves fine-grained threat detection over monolithic guardrails, generalizes better under out-of-domain evaluation, and supports modular expansion.
conclusion: The work highlights task interference in monolithic guardrails and demonstrates the effectiveness of a modular, specialized approach for robust safety in LLMs.

title: Fasr: Automated Identification Of Unsafe Control Actions In Stpa
authors: Ian Dardik, Yining She, Sam Procter, Keaton Hanna, Lutz Wrage, Eunsuk Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is a well-established hazard analysis technique that has been applied to a wide range of safety-critical systems. Despite its popularity, there is relatively little automation support for STPA, and most of its steps are carried out manually by a human analyst, which can be time consuming and error prone. This paper investigates the potential use of model-based engineering and formal methods to assist human analysts in efficiently and accurately carrying out STPA. The proposed tool, called FASR (Formalizing and Automating STPA with Robustness), enables automated, complete identification of unsafe control actions (UCAs), leveraging recent advances in robustness analysis to identify UCAs as undesirable deviations in the controller's actions. The use of the tool is demonstrated on a case study involving a Braking System Control Unit (BSCU) in an avionics system. As a preliminary exploration of the potential benefits and limitations of the tool, the paper reports on a user study involving nine participants with varying backgrounds in STPA, model-based engineering, and formal methods; the study found that most participants considered the tool a useful aid in identifying UCAs, while suggesting improvements that would make a tool such as FASR usable and applicable to a wider range of systems and analysts.
tldr: This paper presents FASR, a tool for automating the identification of unsafe control actions in STPA hazard analysis, applied to an avionics braking system.
motivation: STPA is widely used but lacks automation, making it time-consuming and error-prone. The research aims to improve efficiency and accuracy using model-based engineering and formal methods.
method: The authors developed FASR, which leverages robustness analysis to automatically identify unsafe control actions as deviations in controller actions. A user study with nine participants evaluated the tool.
result: Most participants found FASR useful for identifying UCAs, but suggested improvements for broader applicability and usability.
conclusion: FASR demonstrates potential for automating STPA, but further development is needed to handle diverse systems and analyst backgrounds.

title: Bringing Closure To Theory Combination Properties
authors: Guilherme V. Toledo, Benjamin Przybocki, Yoni Zohar
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30762v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the closure of three classical combination properties, namely, stable infiniteness, gentleness and shininess (or, equivalently for decidable theories, strong politeness), under intersection and combinability. We compute every possible intersection, and then compute the maximal set of theories that can be combined with each resulting intersection. We iterate this process until no new sets are identified. How many properties will we end up with?
tldr: This paper studies closure properties of theory combination properties (stable infiniteness, gentleness, shininess) under intersection and combinability, a topic in mathematical logic and automated reasoning.
motivation: To understand how combination properties behave under intersection and to determine the maximal sets of theories that can be combined, which is relevant for theory combination in satisfiability modulo theories (SMT).
method: The authors compute all possible intersections of the three properties and then determine the maximal set of theories combinable with each intersection, iterating until no new sets are found.
result: The paper identifies the closure of these properties under intersection and combinability, leading to a finite set of resulting properties.
conclusion: The work provides a complete classification of these combination properties, which may impact theory combination techniques in automated reasoning.

title: GaMi: Geometry-Agnostic Material Identification Via Cross-Modal Subtractive Disentanglement
authors: Zhiwei Chen (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Yijie Li (national University Of Singapore, Singapore), Yimo Zhang (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Shiyun Shao (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Yichao Chen (shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Dian Ding (shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China), Liang Wang (northwestern Polytechnical University, Xi'an, China), Haiwei Wu (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Liwei Guo (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Jie Yang (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Xiaosong Zhang (UESTC, Chengdu, China), Yongzhao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-contact material identification enables adaptive interaction for embodied intelligence yet faces challenges from geometry-induced variations (e.g., orientation, shape, distance) and single-modality ambiguities. In this paper, we present GaMi, a multimodal material identification system integrating mmWave and acoustic sensing to robustly operate under unconstrained geometric conditions. By leveraging the insight of shared geometric consistency between co-located bimodal sensors, GaMi employs an intra-sample cross-modal subtractive disentanglement framework. By semantically aligning modalities and subtracting the shared geometric context, it isolates intrinsic material features. Furthermore, GaMi incorporates inter-sample contrastive learning to correct the residual interference caused by cross-modal misalignment. Additionally, a pairing-based adaptation strategy between two modalities enables few-shot generalization across devices. Extensive evaluations on 20 materials show that GaMi achieves 95.2% accuracy, outperforming single-modality baselines across unseen geometric conditions.
tldr: GaMi uses mmWave and acoustic sensing with cross-modal subtractive disentanglement for geometry-agnostic material identification.
motivation: Non-contact material identification is challenged by geometry-induced variations and single-modality ambiguities.
method: Intra-sample cross-modal subtractive disentanglement aligns and subtracts shared geometric context, plus inter-sample contrastive learning and pairing-based adaptation.
result: Achieves 95.2% accuracy on 20 materials, outperforming single-modality baselines across unseen geometric conditions.
conclusion: Demonstrates effective multimodal material identification with few-shot generalization, but no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Send A Scout First: Pre-hoc Reasoning For Adaptive Detector Allocation In Prompt-Injection Defense
authors: Shuhao Zhang, Jiarui Li, Qi Cao, Ruiyi Zhang, Pengtao Xie
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30837v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt-injection detectors are heterogeneous: each is strong on a different slice of attacks, and none is always reliable. Yet existing systems still treat detection as a fixed single-detector pipeline, committing every request to one detector's blind spots. We reframe defense as detector allocation: given a heterogeneous pool, decide per request which detectors to run and whether to escalate to an LLM judge. Our framework SCOUT (Scalable and Controllable Outcome-prediction for Uncertainty-aware Triage) makes this decision dynamic by predicting each detector's per-sample reliability and latency from how it behaved on similar past inputs, and exposes a single safety-utility threshold to the operator (where utility bundles benign-pass rate and wall-clock). To evaluate this setting, we build SCOUT-450, a benchmark that captures the structurally complex, agent-facing injections that older prompt-injection sets under-represent. On SCOUT-450, a safety-oriented operating point reduces attack-success rate by 46% and total wall-clock by 40% relative to an always-on GPT-4o judge, at a 5.1-point benign-utility drop. SCOUT also transfers to three external benchmarks (BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval), improving the safety-utility frontier.
tldr: This paper proposes a dynamic detector allocation framework for prompt-injection defense in LLMs, which is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information and condensed matter physics.
motivation: Existing prompt-injection defenses use fixed single-detector pipelines that are vulnerable to blind spots; the authors aim to improve safety and efficiency by adaptively selecting detectors per request.
method: The SCOUT framework predicts each detector's per-sample reliability and latency based on similar past inputs, and uses a safety-utility threshold to decide which detectors to run and whether to escalate to an LLM judge.
result: On the SCOUT-450 benchmark, a safety-oriented operating point reduces attack-success rate by 46% and wall-clock time by 40% compared to an always-on GPT-4o judge, with a 5.1-point benign-utility drop. It also transfers to three external benchmarks.
conclusion: Dynamic detector allocation improves the safety-utility frontier in prompt-injection defense, but the work is specific to LLM security and has no connection to quantum computing or thermodynamics.

title: Trace: Task-Aware Adaptive Self-Evolving Agentic Jailbreaking
authors: Churui Zeng, Weiwei Qi, Kedong Xiu, Tianhang Zheng, Chaochao Lu, Liang He, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30883v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rise of LLM agents introduces a new threat by enabling planning, coding, and even end-to-end execution of expert-level attack workflows. However, this threat remains underexplored and underestimated since (i) safety alignment prevents LLMs from directly generating harmful instructions, and (ii) most existing jailbreak methods cannot consistently induce agents to execute malicious operations. In this paper, we propose TRACE, a practical agentic jailbreaking framework to further reveal the risks of this threat surface. To conceal the malicious intent, TRACE decomposes a malicious task into multiple subtask sequences under different schemes and selects the sequence with the fewest explicitly harmful subtasks. TRACE then disguises the remaining harmful subtasks as benign-looking instructions by embedding them in task-aware scenarios with related roles, environments, directives, and heuristics. The scenarios are iteratively evolved through well-defined transformation actions, which are sampled by a Q-learning-inspired mechanism, for inducing the agent to execute on the harmful subtasks. Extensive evaluations on AgentHarm and AdvCUA show that TRACE consistently outperforms existing jailbreak baselines across multiple advanced LLM agents, achieving up to 100% bypass rate and 0.73 average success score. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of TRACE in controlled cyberattack instances. Our code and demos are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper proposes TRACE, a framework for jailbreaking LLM agents by decomposing malicious tasks into subtask sequences and disguising them as benign instructions.
motivation: To reveal the underexplored threat of LLM agents being used for expert-level attack workflows, despite safety alignment and existing jailbreak methods.
method: TRACE decomposes malicious tasks into subtask sequences, selects the sequence with fewest harmful subtasks, disguises remaining harmful subtasks as benign-looking instructions within task-aware scenarios, and iteratively evolves scenarios using Q-learning-inspired transformations.
result: TRACE achieves up to 100% bypass rate and 0.73 average success score on AgentHarm and AdvCUA benchmarks, outperforming existing jailbreak baselines across multiple advanced LLM agents.
conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical agentic jailbreaking method, highlighting significant security risks in LLM agents and the need for improved defenses.

title: A Core-Structure-Based Automated Analysis Tool For Commercial Virtualization Obfuscation Deobfuscation
authors: Wanju Kim, Seoksu Lee, Eun-Sun Cho
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Virtualization obfuscation is a more powerful obfuscation technique compared to other obfuscation methods, and as it is increasingly being applied to malware, it demands significant effort and time from analysts. This study analyzes virtualization obfuscation and proposes a tool called VMPredator that automatically extracts semantic units. The proposed tool performs various analyses including memory analysis and trace analysis, while minimizing dependency on the specific internal structure of virtual machines in order to handle diverse forms of virtualization obfuscation that existing tools are unable to process. Experimental results demonstrate that the length of obfuscated programs was reduced by approximately 85%, and it was verified through validation that small-scale programs were fully restored to semantics identical to the original.
tldr: This paper presents VMPredator, a tool for deobfuscating virtualization-obfuscated code, with no connection to quantum computing or information thermodynamics.
motivation: Virtualization obfuscation is increasingly used in malware, making analysis difficult; existing tools cannot handle diverse forms.
method: The tool performs memory analysis and trace analysis while minimizing dependency on specific VM structures to automatically extract semantic units.
result: Obfuscated program length reduced by ~85%; small-scale programs fully restored to original semantics.
conclusion: VMPredator effectively automates deobfuscation of virtualization-obfuscated code, but its applicability to large-scale programs and novel obfuscation techniques remains to be tested.

title: Free-Riding In The Ai Economy: Demystifying Logic Flaws In x402-Enabled Payment Systems
authors: Shengchen Ling, Yihang Huang, Yuan Chen, Yajin Zhou, Lei Wu, Cong Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.30998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The agentic economy demands programmatic financial rails, positioning the x402 protocol as the de facto standard for machine-to-machine payments. However, bridging synchronous HTTP requests with asynchronous blockchain finality introduces profound state synchronization challenges. In this work, we perform the first comprehensive security analysis of the x402 ecosystem. By formalizing five Security Invariants, we reveal that current implementations fail to enforce transactional atomicity and cryptographic context binding, leading to systemic vulnerabilities. We identify a semantic gap in signature design enabling cross-resource substitution, where payment proofs are transplanted to other unauthorized contexts. Furthermore, we expose a temporal gap where concurrency race conditions allow probabilistic service duplication. In the AI inference domain, we demonstrate how dynamic pricing models are vulnerable to allowance overdrafts and infrastructure rate limits. We validate these vulnerabilities against official SDKs and live deployments. Specifically, we show that attackers can exploit the synchronization gap in dynamic authorization schemes to force merchants to subsidize compute costs, achieving a resource leakage ratio of up to 100% on production middleware. Finally, we propose architectural mitigations, advocating for request-bound signatures and pessimistic state locking to secure the financial rails of autonomous agents. All discovered issues have been disclosed to Coinbase and ThirdWeb.
tldr: This paper analyzes security vulnerabilities in the x402 payment protocol for AI agent economies, focusing on state synchronization and cryptographic flaws.
motivation: The rise of agentic economies requires secure machine-to-machine payment systems, but the x402 protocol's bridging of synchronous HTTP and asynchronous blockchain introduces vulnerabilities.
method: The authors formalize five Security Invariants, analyze official SDKs and live deployments, and demonstrate attacks like cross-resource substitution and concurrency race conditions.
result: They identify semantic and temporal gaps enabling resource leakage up to 100% on production middleware, including allowance overdrafts and service duplication.
conclusion: Proposed mitigations include request-bound signatures and pessimistic state locking; issues disclosed to Coinbase and ThirdWeb.

title: Thou Shall Not Pass: Gatekeeping Outbound Tls Connections
authors: Henrique B. Brum, Matteo Franzil, Riccardo Germenia, Salvatore Manfredi, Domenico Siracusa, Luis A. Dias Knob
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite the widespread use of Transport Layer Security (TLS), its security guarantees are frequently compromised by outdated versions and misconfigurations. To analyze this problem, we collected more than 50 million TLS handshakes over a two-week period at our research institution, Fondazione Bruno Kessler, and analyzed three server-selected parameters against the recommendations of four TLS guidelines. Our analysis shows that while the use of insecure or outdated options is minimal, it remains persistent. More importantly, servers are adopting the latest TLS advancements much faster than official guidelines can be updated to provide directives for them. These findings, combined with the difficulty of configuring TLS clients due to their ephemeral, ubiquitous and server-dependent nature, leave users vulnerable to non-standard or outright insecure connections. To address this, we present TLSGatekeeper, a real-time, network-based tool that transparently monitors handshakes, analyzes server parameters, and, based on organizational policy, reports non-compliant connections without requiring client-side modifications. Unlike Next-Generation Firewalls, TLSGatekeeper preserves end-to-end privacy by validating only handshakes, and offers greater flexibility in defining undesired configurations. Our evaluation shows that TLSGatekeeper sustains traffic rates of up to 100 Gbps while preventing insecure connections, with an average added processing delay of 671 ns (TLS 1.3) and 795 ns (TLS 1.2) per handshake packet, making enforcement feasible at scale.
tldr: This paper presents TLSGatekeeper, a network tool for monitoring and enforcing TLS handshake compliance without client-side modifications.
motivation: TLS security is often compromised by outdated versions and misconfigurations, and clients are difficult to configure due to their ephemeral nature.
method: The authors collected over 50 million TLS handshakes, analyzed server parameters against guidelines, and developed TLSGatekeeper, a real-time network-based tool that transparently monitors handshakes and reports non-compliant connections.
result: Insecure options are minimal but persistent; servers adopt new TLS advancements faster than guidelines update. TLSGatekeeper sustains 100 Gbps with sub-microsecond added delay.
conclusion: TLSGatekeeper provides scalable enforcement of TLS policies while preserving end-to-end privacy, but the paper focuses on network security, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: R+r: Reassessing Java Security Api Misuse In Current LLMs: A Replication On Jca And Jsse APIs With External Security Knowledge
authors: Tianhe Lu (school Of Computer Science, University Of Auckland, New Zealand), Eric Spero (school Of Computer Science, University Of Auckland, New Zealand), Sakuna Harinda Jayasundara (school Of Computer Science, University Of Auckland, New Zealand), Robert Biddle (school Of Computer Science, University Of Auckland, New Zealand), Giovanni Russello
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The misuse of Java security APIs is a serious security problem in software development. Research in 2024 has shown that this problem is widespread in LLM-generated code. However, it remains unclear whether this phenomenon persists in current models and how external security knowledge affects it. This paper presents a scoped replication and extension of Mousavi et al.'s study on the Java Cryptography Architecture (JCA) and Java Secure Socket Extension (JSSE) APIs. We focus on two complementary settings: GPT-5.5 as a frontier proprietary coding model, and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct as a strong open-weight model relevant to self-hosted deployment. The results show that although newer LLMs perform better in using Java security APIs, the problem of Java security API misuse has not been eliminated. External security knowledge substantially improves the measured outcome, but its effect is model-dependent. For Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, secure code examples are the most effective single knowledge type. For GPT-5.5, explicit misuse patterns eliminate all detected security API misuses among valid programs in our benchmark, although some outputs remain invalid due to compilation errors or target-API mismatches. In addition, developer-guide knowledge becomes much more effective, and secure prompting also provides large gains for GPT-5.5. Overall, these findings confirm the Java security API misuse risk identified in the original study and show that the benefits of retrieval-augmented knowledge depend not only on the knowledge itself and retrieval behavior, but also on model capability.
tldr: This paper studies misuse of Java security APIs in code generated by LLMs, finding that newer models still produce insecure code but external security knowledge can reduce misuse.
motivation: Previous research showed widespread misuse of Java security APIs in LLM-generated code; this work replicates and extends that study to assess current models and the impact of external security knowledge.
method: The authors replicate Mousavi et al.'s study on JCA and JSSE APIs, testing GPT-5.5 and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct with various types of external security knowledge (secure code examples, misuse patterns, developer guides, secure prompting).
result: Newer LLMs perform better but still exhibit API misuse; external knowledge improves outcomes but effects are model-dependent. For GPT-5.5, explicit misuse patterns eliminated all detected misuses among valid programs, though some outputs had compilation errors.
conclusion: Java security API misuse risk persists in current LLMs; retrieval-augmented knowledge benefits depend on both knowledge type and model capability, suggesting tailored approaches for different models.

title: EvoDefense: Co-Evolving Black-Box Defense With Large Language Models
authors: Yu Li, Yuenan Hou, Yingmei Wei, Yanming Guo, Chaochao Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) remain highly vulnerable to diverse attacks, particularly in black-box settings where the internals of target models are inaccessible. Existing black-box defenses typically rely on pre-defined filtering heuristics, which often fail to generalize to unseen attack types and target model architectures. We introduce EvoDefense, an experience-guided co-evolving black-box defense paradigm. EvoDefense employs a guard LLM to detect malicious queries and an experience memory module to accumulate defense knowledge from previous interactions. At the core of EvoDefense is a continuous attack-defense evolution loop, where an attack generator and the guard model iteratively refine their attack strategies and defense policies through experience-guided optimization. This design enables EvoDefense to generalize across unseen attacks and target models without retraining. Experiments on HarmBench, AdvBench, and AlpacaEval show that EvoDefense achieves consistently strong defense performance across seven popular models and five representative LLM attacks, while preserving competitive general capabilities. On HarmBench, EvoDefense reduces the attack success rate (ASR) of AutoDAN-turbo on Gemini-3-flash and LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct from 29.4% and 43.4% to 8.4% and 6.2%, respectively.
tldr: EvoDefense is a co-evolving black-box defense for LLMs using a guard LLM and experience memory to adapt to unseen attacks.
motivation: Existing black-box defenses rely on pre-defined heuristics that fail to generalize to new attack types and target models.
method: EvoDefense uses a guard LLM to detect malicious queries, an experience memory module to accumulate defense knowledge, and an attack-defense evolution loop where an attack generator and the guard model iteratively refine strategies.
result: EvoDefense reduces attack success rates significantly on HarmBench, AdvBench, and AlpacaEval across seven models and five attacks, e.g., from 29.4% to 8.4% on Gemini-3-flash.
conclusion: The approach demonstrates strong generalization without retraining, but its relevance to quantum computing or information thermodynamics is negligible.

title: MAECO-Lite: Modular Ontology For Dynamic Malware Analysis
authors: Zekeri Adams, Peter \v{s}vec, J\'an K\v{l}uka, Roderik Ploszek, Monday Onoja, \v{s}tefan Balogh, Martin Homola
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31199v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Capturing dynamic malware behavior in a practical but still semantically precise manner remains a significant challenge in cyber threat intelligence. While standards such as MAEC and STIX provide widely adopted vocabularies for describing malware artifacts and observations, they represent data with considerable complexity in structures that often obscure important ontological distinctions. In particular, they tend to conflate enduring malware artifacts with the events generated during execution, thereby flattening distinctions that are central in foundational standards for ontology design. In this paper, we conduct a foundational ontological analysis of core MAEC and STIX constructs relevant to dynamic malware analysis relying on Unified Foundational Ontology (UFO) as a theoretical lens. Our analysis reveals some ontological mismatches arising from the conflation of artifacts, dispositions, and runtime events in MAEC and STIX that complicate coherent representation of dynamic malware behavior and, from a practical perspective, limit the ability to reason about execution traces. Based on these insights, we propose MAECO-Lite, a lightweight ontology designed to represent data and operationalize their processing for dynamic malware analysis. The ontology adopts a modular structure centered on samples, processes, actions, system artifacts, and MITRE ATT&CK Techniques, while maintaining a clear separation between enduring entities and runtime events. An initial evaluation using description logic concept learning algorithms shows that the simplified ontology significantly improves learning performance, demonstrating that ontologically grounded modelling can enhance both semantic clarity and computational usability.
tldr: This paper presents MAECO-Lite, a lightweight ontology for dynamic malware analysis, grounded in foundational ontology principles to improve semantic clarity and computational usability.
motivation: Existing standards like MAEC and STIX conflate enduring malware artifacts with runtime events, complicating coherent representation and reasoning about dynamic malware behavior.
method: The authors conduct a foundational ontological analysis of MAEC and STIX using the Unified Foundational Ontology (UFO), then propose MAECO-Lite with a modular structure separating enduring entities and events, and evaluate it using description logic concept learning algorithms.
result: MAECO-Lite significantly improves learning performance compared to the original MAEC/STIX representations, demonstrating that ontologically grounded modeling enhances both semantic clarity and computational usability.
conclusion: The work shows the benefits of applying foundational ontology to cybersecurity, but its focus on malware analysis is unrelated to the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: BadBone: Backdoor Attacks Against Backbone Models In Visual Prompt Learning
authors: Ziqing Yang, Rui Wen, Xinlei He, Yun Shen, Michael Backes, Yang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31246v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prompt learning is a new machine learning paradigm that has attracted ample attention due to its simplicity and proven efficacy. Despite its growing adoption, the security vulnerabilities associated with this paradigm remain underexplored. In this work, we take the first step to propose BadBone, a stealthy and adaptive backdoor attack against prompt learning using bi-level optimization. Instead of backdooring the prompt learning process, we aim to compromise a backbone model such that only target downstream tasks employing prompt learning inherit the backdoor vulnerability. Extensive experiments on three different models and three datasets from various domains show that our targeted/untargeted backdoored models achieve high attack performance while maintaining utility on both pre-training and downstream tasks. Moreover, we evaluate our approach against six state-of-the-art model-level defenses, including Neural Cleanse, ABS, MNTD, NAD, CLP, and D-BR. The results demonstrate that these defenses are largely ineffective against our backdoored models and thus leave the effective defense as an important direction for future work.
tldr: This paper proposes a backdoor attack against backbone models used in visual prompt learning, but it is unrelated to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning for physics.
motivation: The security vulnerabilities of prompt learning in machine learning are underexplored, and the authors aim to demonstrate a stealthy backdoor attack.
method: BadBone uses bi-level optimization to compromise a backbone model so that downstream tasks using prompt learning inherit the backdoor.
result: The attack achieves high performance on three models and datasets, and six state-of-the-art defenses are largely ineffective.
conclusion: Effective defenses against such backdoor attacks remain an important direction for future work.

title: Envy Cycle Elimination With Strategic Agents: Best Responses And Fairness Guarantees
authors: Georgios Amanatidis, Georgios Birmpas, Rebecca Reiffenh\"auser
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With strong evidence in the literature showing that fairness and truthfulness are incompatible, there is a recent line of work focusing on the fairness properties of equilibria of simple fair division mechanisms, especially Round-Robin. We consider the Envy Cycle Elimination (E-C-E) procedure of Lipton et al. [23], one of the most versatile tools in fair division. While this simple and intuitive algorithm achieves allocations that are envy-free up to one item (EF1) for any number of agents and general monotone valuation functions, surprisingly little is known about its behavior when agents act strategically. We demonstrate how the presence of incentives, although highly natural and relevant for the majority of applications, completely removes the intuitive clarity in the algorithm's execution, even for a few agents and very simple valuation functions. Additionally, while in the standard algorithmic setting there is great flexibility in how the details of E-C-E are implemented, here additional specifications are needed before the procedure is clearly defined, the choice of which has a potentially huge impact on the agents' behavior. Despite these obstacles, for various natural versions of E-C-E, we give the first results on the existence of Pure Nash Equilibria of the resulting mechanisms, and show there exist versions where fairness guarantees are approximately preserved for agents who play best responses.
tldr: This paper studies strategic behavior and fairness guarantees in the Envy Cycle Elimination procedure for fair division, but is unrelated to quantum computing or the user's research interests.
motivation: To understand how strategic agents affect the fairness of the Envy Cycle Elimination algorithm, which is known to be EF1 under truthful behavior.
method: Game-theoretic analysis of different versions of the E-C-E procedure, proving existence of Pure Nash Equilibria and approximate fairness guarantees.
result: Strategic behavior can break the intuitive clarity of E-C-E, but some versions still have equilibria that approximately preserve fairness.
conclusion: The choice of tie-breaking and other specifications greatly impacts strategic outcomes; future work may explore other mechanisms.

title: MeshGuard: MUD-Based Network Access Control For Large-Scale Thread-Powered IoT Networks
authors: Dominik Roy George, Wouter van Hoof, Habib Mostafaei, Savio Sciancalepore
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The IETF standard Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) enables manufacturers to equip IoT devices with certified URLs that provide traffic profiles for those devices, helping administrators enforce network access control. However, MUD assumes devices operate on full IP stacks and therefore does not account for constrained IoT devices running Thread--the dominant low-power mesh networking standard--which lacks complete TCP/IP functionality. While prior work proposes extensions to support MUD in Thread environments, these approaches are limited to simple topologies with a single border router and do not scale to realistic deployments with multiple, heterogeneous border routers. We introduce MeshGuard, a framework enabling MUD-based access control in complex Thread networks, with any number of border routers. MeshGuard extends the Mesh Link Establishment (MLE) protocol to deliver MUD information from constrained devices to border routers regardless of network topology. Moreover, MeshGuard leverages Software-Defined Networking (SDN) to synchronize access control lists across all routers. Experiments on our proof-of-concept with real devices (nRF5340, nRF52833, Raspberry-Pi 3) demonstrate enhanced security, minimal overhead, and linear scalability compared to state-of-the-art approaches.
tldr: MeshGuard extends MUD-based network access control to large-scale Thread IoT networks using SDN.
motivation: Existing MUD approaches do not support constrained Thread devices in complex multi-border-router topologies.
method: MeshGuard extends the MLE protocol to deliver MUD information and uses SDN to synchronize ACLs across routers.
result: Proof-of-concept experiments show enhanced security, minimal overhead, and linear scalability.
conclusion: MeshGuard enables scalable MUD-based access control for Thread networks, but further real-world testing is needed.

title: Toward Accessible Mobile Money: A Voice-Driven, Biometrically Secured Ussd Automation Framework For Visually Impaired Users
authors: Sunday Ajayi, Babatunde Eric Olatunji, Eric Umuhoza
abstract: ArXiv:2605.31375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial inclusion has expanded significantly across Africa through mobile money services delivered primarily via USSD technology. However, visually impaired individuals continue to face accessibility and security barriers when conducting financial transactions. Current USSD systems are not designed for non-visual interaction, forcing users to rely on third-party assistance even for PIN entry, thereby increasing fraud exposure and reducing transaction confidence. Although alternative assistive technologies such as screen readers exist, they are not compatible with USSD operations, often causing sessions to time out before the user can complete a transaction. This paper presents an Android-based intelligent middleware that automates USSD transactions, integrates biometric-secured PIN injection, and introduces a privacy-preserving screen-dimming mechanism: Blackout Mode. The system leverages Android Accessibility Services, hardware-backed Keystore security, and on-device natural language parsing to enable independent, secure voice-based mobile money access. We show that the proposed solution improves task success rates from 65-75% to more than 90% and reduces transaction completion time from 40-60 seconds to 12-15 seconds, while also improving perceived security.
tldr: This paper presents an Android middleware that automates USSD transactions with biometric security and voice interaction for visually impaired users.
motivation: Visually impaired users face accessibility and security barriers with current USSD mobile money systems, relying on third-party assistance that increases fraud risk.
method: The system uses Android Accessibility Services, hardware-backed Keystore, and on-device natural language parsing to automate USSD flows, inject biometric PINs, and dim the screen (Blackout Mode) for privacy.
result: Task success rates improved from 65-75% to over 90%, and transaction completion time reduced from 40-60 seconds to 12-15 seconds, with enhanced perceived security.
conclusion: The framework demonstrates a practical solution for accessible mobile money, but its relevance to quantum computing, condensed matter physics, or machine learning is negligible.

title: Bers: Locally Optimal Continuous Algorithm For Maritime Weather Routing With Just-in-Time Arrival
authors: Daniel Precioso, Francisco Su\'arez, Javier Jim\'enez de la Jara, Rafael Ballester-Ripoll, David G\'omez-Ullate
abstract:
ArXiv:2605.31533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Maritime weather routing must optimize route geometry under dynamic wind-wave conditions, obstacle constraints, and fixed-arrival requirements. We present B'ezier Evolve and Refine Strategy (
ame{}), a two-stage framework that combines global evolutionary search (CMA-ES) with local variational refinement (FMS). Routes are parametrized as B'ezier curves and evaluated with dense along-path sampling, enabling smooth trajectories while preserving practical feasibility constraints and accounting for mid-segment effects. We evaluate 
ame{} on synthetic benchmarks designed to stress seven operational criteria: continuity, obstacle avoidance, dynamic adaptation, flexible objective design, constant-load feasibility, just-in-time arrival, and local optimality. Across these tests, 
ame{} matches or improves published baselines while maintaining robust convergence under challenging flow fields and land geometries. We then validate the method on real ocean data using hourly ERA5 forcing over 366 daily departures in 2024 for two trans-oceanic corridors (Atlantic and Pacific), with a physics-based model of an 88~m cargo vessel with optional rigid wingsails. In real-ocean experiments, route optimization alone reduces mean propulsive energy by 23--59\% versus great-circle baselines of the same propulsion mode. Combined with wind-assisted propulsion, total savings reach up to 75\%. These results show that 
ame{} provides a practical and scalable foundation for just-in-time, energy-efficient weather routing in maritime decarbonization workflows.
tldr: This paper presents a two-stage optimization framework for maritime weather routing using Bézier curves and evolutionary search, achieving significant energy savings.
motivation: To develop a practical and scalable method for just-in-time, energy-efficient maritime weather routing that accounts for dynamic conditions and operational constraints.
method: The method combines global evolutionary search (CMA-ES) with local variational refinement (FMS), parametrizing routes as Bézier curves and evaluating them with dense along-path sampling.
result: On synthetic benchmarks, the method matches or improves baselines; on real ocean data, it reduces mean propulsive energy by 23-59% versus great-circle baselines, with total savings up to 75% when combined with wind-assisted propulsion.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical foundation for just-in-time, energy-efficient weather routing, contributing to maritime decarbonization.
